top.title: Archaeologists discover 1,200-year-old mummified hairless dog in Peru
top.summary: Archaeologists have discovered 1,200-year-old remains of Peru’s famous hairless dogs at an ancient Wari Empire burial site, including remarkably preserved mummies and puppies buried alongside humans. Their unusual teeth, diets, and burial arrangements reveal surprising clues about how ancient Peruvians cared for, bred, and sometimes discarded their dogs.
top.text: Archaeologists working at an ancient burial complex in Peru have uncovered remarkable evidence of hairless dogs that lived more than 1,200 years ago, long before the rise of the Inca Empire. The discoveries include naturally mummified remains, unusual skeletal features, and clues about what the animals ate and how they were treated by the people around them. Peruvian hairless dogs are a distinctive Indigenous breed known for their slender bodies, pointed ears, and lack of fur. They frequently appear in pottery created by ancient societies along the Andean coast. Today, a variation of the breed is recognized by the American Kennel Club as the Peruvian Inca Orchid. The dogs are also an important national symbol, having been officially designated part of Peru's cultural heritage in 2000. A study published in the Journal of Anthropological Archaeology reports the first physical evidence of Peruvian hairless dogs at Castillo de Huarmey, the only known Wari Empire site discovered so far on Peru's northern coast. Located approximately 190 miles north of Lima, Castillo de Huarmey covers 110 acres and once served as an administrative and burial center for the Wari Empire. The complex was occupied between 600 and 1050 CE, roughly 400 years before the Inca rose to power. The site has already produced several extraordinary archaeological discoveries. In 2012, researchers uncovered the first undisturbed elite Wari tomb, containing the remains of 58 high-status women, six human sacrifices, and approximately 1,300 artifacts. Another important discovery followed in 2022, when archaeologists identified nearby burials of elite craftspeople accompanied by gold, silver, and bronze tools. Together, these findings have helped researchers understand how the Wari Empire governed its territories. The newly examined dog remains offer a different perspective on daily life at the site, particularly the complicated relationships between people and animals. "Our findings indicate that humans and dogs coexisted at this Wari site, but reconstructing their bond is challenging, as past emotions are difficult to capture through archaeological methods," says first author Weronika Tomczyk, a research associate in Dartmouth's Department of Anthropology and a postdoctoral fellow in its Ecology, Evolution, Environment and Society Program. "The goal of our study was to not only present data on Castillo de Huarmey's dog burials, but also emphasize that people in the past had often contradictory relationships with the animals, just as they do today: a pet for one group of people could at the same time be considered a pest by their closest neighbors." Remarkably Preserved Dog Mummies Found in the Peruvian Desert Castillo de Huarmey lies in an extremely dry region of Peru's Pacific coast. The desert's exceptionally arid conditions have helped preserve materials that would normally deteriorate over time, including hair, bones, clothing, leather, pigments, and decorated pottery. Among the artifacts recovered from the site is an unusual ceramic vessel depicting a seated Peruvian hairless dog with humanlike features. The animal appears to be holding an object resembling a musical instrument. Between 2010 and 2025, excavations also uncovered numerous remains of South American camelids, probably domesticated llamas and alpacas. Some may have been deposited as offerings during funerary ceremonies, while others appear to have been discarded as waste. Archaeologists also recovered the skeletal remains of dogs. However, interpreting these discoveries has been complicated by extensive damage and looting. A powerful earthquake in 1970 caused part of Castillo de Huarmey to collapse, exposing burial chambers containing pottery and other valuable objects. Looters subsequently disturbed large sections of the complex. The deeper archaeological layers remained untouched and retained their original Wari context. In contrast, the upper layers, where most of the animal remains were discovered, contained materials that had become mixed together. During excavations in the northern section of the main ceremonial area, three sets of dog remains stood out. One was a naturally mummified skull that still retained visible hairless skin and attached ears. The skull had also been colored with cinnabar, a bright red pigment commonly used in ancient Peruvian funerary traditions. Researchers discovered a second, larger dog skull, along with the naturally mummified skeleton of a male dog buried in a shallow pit. The male skeleton was almost complete, missing only the lower portions of its front limbs. At first, the researchers suspected that the mummified dog might have been buried relatively recently, perhaps around 50 years earlier during the period of looting. But Tomczyk noticed two important details: the animal was hairless, and all three dogs lacked their first premolars. The missing teeth provided an unexpected clue that helped researchers identify the animals. "What I noticed is that some of the dog skeletons were missing teeth, and not that they lost them during their lifespan; some teeth, especially first premolars and sometimes last molars, had just never erupted," said Tomczyk. "And then I found in the literature that the same gene which is responsible for hairlessness in dogs is responsible for a reduced number of teeth, indicating that these were Peruvian hairless dogs." In other words, the animals were not necessarily missing teeth because of injury, disease, or old age. Their reduced number of teeth was linked to the same genetic trait responsible for their hairlessness. This distinctive biological connection offered evidence that the remains belonged to Peruvian hairless dogs rather than other ancient dog populations. To investigate further, the researchers applied standard zooarchaeological techniques, which involve studying animal remains recovered from archaeological sites. These methods helped them estimate the ages of the dogs and examine their physical characteristics. The team also analyzed chemical signatures preserved in the animals' bones and teeth. Known as isotopic analysis, this technique can reveal information about what an animal ate and drank, as well as where it may have lived. The researchers examined isotopes of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and strontium. These are different forms of chemical elements that can preserve clues about diet and environmental conditions. Strontium is particularly useful because its composition varies with local geology and can help scientists trace an animal's geographic origins or movements. The results were compared with similar measurements from human and camelid remains recovered at Castillo de Huarmey. "Isotopic analyses of a dog's tooth give a signal of its life as a puppy because dog teeth erupt so fast, and the bone gives a signal of more or less the last year of its life," said Tomczyk. "Such sampling strategy aimed to provide signals from distinct stages of a dog's life." Altogether, the excavations produced 341 dog bone specimens representing at least 19 individual dogs, in addition to the complete mummified male dog. Some of the remains were found in particularly intriguing burial contexts. For example, the bones of a puppy estimated to have been just 6 to 8 weeks old were discovered alongside an elite craftsperson nicknamed the "Master Basketmaker." Other finds included the bones of an adult dog buried within the site's palace and part of a puppy skeleton buried with a male individual identified as XY, who was probably sacrificed to serve as a tomb guardian. Most of the dogs were adults at the time of burial. However, their remains suggest that the animals did not all receive the same treatment. Some appear to have been deliberately buried, potentially reflecting a special role in Wari society. Others were found among discarded materials. Only a small number of bones displayed butchery marks, suggesting that dogs were not commonly consumed as food. Radio

top.title: Scientists predicted doomsday for November 13, 2026. Should we be worried?
top.summary: In 1960, scientists predicted that runaway population growth would bring humanity to the brink of destruction on November 13, 2026, and their mathematical forecasts remained surprisingly accurate for decades. But as birth rates declined and population growth slowed, the terrifying prediction unraveled, revealing how even convincing scientific models can fail when human behavior changes.
top.text: In 1960, Science , one of the world’s leading science journals, published an article with an unambiguous title: Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026 . It predicted that on this future date — less than a month from today — the human population would approach infinity and effectively annihilate itself. The outlandishness of the claim landed the article widespread public attention . More surprisingly — because its underlying research and math seemed sound — it also received careful and sustained scientific attention. The authors — Heinz von Foerster , an Austrian-American professor and cybernetics expert and two of his students, Patricia M. Mora and Lawrence W. Amiot — argued that human populations are exceptional and might grow beyond an exponential rate, at an ever-increasing one. “Our great-great-grandchildren will not starve,” they argued. “They will be squeezed to death.” The article was regularly cited, and its predictions appeared remarkably accurate — until around 1993, halfway to the predicted “doomsday,” when the global population began falling behind its forecasts. Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half what it was in 1960 . Hopefully, we will all wake up on Nov. 13 to an ordinary day. Nonetheless, this article remains exemplary for blending rigorous science with the art of stagecraft to staggering effect. The mid-20th century saw increasing societal concern about global population growth and its potential to lead to resource scarcity and geopolitical conflict. Underlying much of this concern was implicit or explicit acceptance of the Malthusian idea that whereas population has the potential to grow exponentially, it is kept constantly under check by its capacity to feed itself . In their article, however, von Foerster and his co-authors argued that as far as populations go, humans may be exceptional. Given our capacity to communicate and form “coalitions” that help us resolve problems, rising population density might simply mean more opportunities for collaboration, so that our numbers might grow not only beyond an exponential rate but at an ever-increasing one. They then used 24 estimates of the world population stretching across the past 2,000 years to show that human numbers have in fact continually outpaced expectations. All this was presented in calm, scientific prose and aided by dense mathematical equations. Von Foerster and his co-authors then projected these historical figures into the future, calculating that thanks to ever-increasing growth, in the year 2026 our numbers would near infinity. Thankfully, the same capacity for collaboration that assisted our species’ development throughout history could now avert this catastrophe. Since we are unlikely to want to reduce our life spans, they concluded, we should work together to reduce the global birth rate by half. This publication caused an immediate stir. There were stories in Time and The New York Times . It became the subject of a series of Pogo comic strips and many commentators took the article as strictly a tongue-in-cheek comment on population fears. Rather than the story dying out, a funny thing happened. When Science published letters to the editor from mathematicians and demographers attacking von Foerster and his colleagues’ work — calling it “ridiculous” and “manifestly absurd” — the authors responded with spirited defenses that doubled down on the underlying math and its conclusions. Throughout the 1960s through to the 1980s, the “doomsday” equation became regularly cited — usually at face value — in textbooks on genetics, ecology and demography. It appeared in stranger places, too. In a 1963 Canadian Parliamentary committee , for example, a witness from the chemical industry prominently cited it as reason chemical pesticides were required: to feed the approaching population explosion. In a 1971 U.S. Supreme Court abortion case leading up to Roe v. Wade, it was cited as why there was no compelling reason for the government to favor increased population. The doomsday idea persisted in part because its predictions for future populations turned out to be highly accurate — at least for a while. Its core equation yielded projections that were better than those of most demographers throughout the 1970s and 1980s . Only around 1993 did that accuracy begin to falter and the global population began falling behind the forecasts — because the world began to do what von Foerster and his colleagues recommended it do. Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half the 1960 rate. We will probably not all wake up on Friday, Nov. 13 “squeezed to death.” But before simply moving on — prepping for the next doomsday scenario — it is worth asking what we can learn from this one. For me, the lesson is in how we present our beliefs to the world. Heinz von Foerster was, at one point in his life, a stage magician . Borrowing the classic language of stagecraft, an effective illusion relies on three parts: the setup, the extraordinary turn and the final reveal that returns the situation to normal. Von Foerster and his co-authors’ article gained attention because it was an ordinary scientific article wrapped in an extraordinary title and conclusion. It retained significance because it was firmly grounded in research and argument. To draw the world’s attention to a serious matter by way of absurdity — that’s a good trick. top.title: James Webb reveals a strange bulge in an alien planet's atmosphere
top.summary: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have discovered that a distant alien planet's atmosphere is surprisingly lopsided. Located 1,300 light-years away, the scorching gas giant WASP-17b experiences powerful winds that redistribute heat, causing one side of its atmosphere to bulge outward. A groundbreaking new mapping technique revealed these hidden distortions, confirming predictions about how extreme temperatures and winds shape alien worlds.
top.text: Astronomers have long depicted distant exoplanets with smooth, circular outlines. But new observations reveal that the atmospheres surrounding some of these scorching alien worlds can have surprisingly uneven shapes. Using NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), researchers have discovered that the atmosphere of WASP-17b, a giant planet roughly 1,300 light-years from Earth, extends farther outward on one side than the other. Although its overall outline remains approximately circular, its atmosphere is noticeably asymmetrical. The distortion provides new evidence of how extreme temperatures and powerful winds reshape the atmospheres of distant planets. The discovery, published in Nature Astronomy , comes from a study jointly led by Cornell University in the United States and the University of Bristol in the United Kingdom. Researchers used an innovative technique called 'transmission strings', developed by Bristol astrophysicists Dr. David Grant and Dr. Hannah Wakeford, to investigate the planet's atmospheric structure in unprecedented detail. WASP-17b belongs to a class of planets known as 'hot Jupiters', enormous gas giants that orbit close to their host stars and experience intense heating. Its unusual atmospheric shape offers a new perspective on how heat moves around these extreme worlds. Lead author Dr. Lili Alderson, a Klarman Postdoctoral Fellow at Cornell University, began the research while studying at the University of Bristol, where she earned her doctorate in physics. "This is proof of concept that planets are in fact 3D objects, and that consistently, as they go around their star, what we predict should be happening is happening. To move beyond computational exercises and see it for real is a different matter." The observations provide valuable information about WASP-17b's atmospheric chemistry and temperature variations, including differences between its equator and poles and between its permanently illuminated and dark hemispheres. These results closely match earlier theoretical predictions and computer models. Together, they offer one of the most detailed three-dimensional pictures of an exoplanet's atmosphere yet produced, establishing a useful reference point for studying the more than 6,000 exoplanets confirmed so far. Co-author Dr. Hannah Wakeford, Associate Professor in Astrophysics at the University of Bristol, said: "Planets are temperamental, their atmospheres complex and chaotic. The fact that all of these numbers came together and showed us this very structured, dynamical picture of this giant world over 1,000 light-years away was just really exciting." James Webb's extraordinary sensitivity has already enabled scientists to investigate alien atmospheres using a method called eclipse mapping. This approach examines subtle changes in light as a planet moves behind its parent star, helping researchers determine how conditions vary across the planet. The new "transmission strings" technique, also called transit mapping, examines the opposite part of the planet's orbit. As an exoplanet passes in front of its star, some starlight travels through the outer edges of its atmosphere before reaching the telescope. By analyzing that light from different angles, scientists can investigate the atmosphere's composition and determine how far it extends at different locations around the planet. This outer atmospheric boundary is known as the limb. Traditional methods generally combine light measurements from the entire limb into a single average spectrum. The new approach instead separates information from different regions, allowing researchers to identify atmospheric variations that would otherwise be concealed. "Rather than assuming your atmosphere is a circle with the same radius all the way around, our technique allows you to pull out different distances from the center to the edge of the planet," Dr. Alderson said. "We're able to go around the edge. So, we've gone from a ring to understanding where on the ring the gemstones are, so to speak." The new measurements revealed a particularly interesting feature near WASP-17b's equator, precisely where previous models predicted it would appear. The distortion occurs on the planet's "evening" side, where powerful atmospheric winds carry heat away from the hemisphere that permanently faces its star and toward the hemisphere locked in darkness. This movement of hot gas causes the atmosphere on the evening side to expand farther outward than it does on the cooler "morning" side. As a result, the planet's atmospheric outline is not perfectly symmetrical. The findings confirm a major prediction about the temperature differences between these regions. The transit mapping measurements also supported other previously identified characteristics of WASP-17b. Dr. Alderson added: "Theory predicts that the morning and the evening sides should have a strong temperature difference, and WASP-17b fits really nicely in that trend -- pretty much bang-on what we thought it would be." Successfully applying transmission strings to WASP-17b demonstrates that the technique could be used to study the atmospheres of many other exoplanets. Until recently, much of what astronomers could determine about these distant atmospheres came from measurements averaged across large regions. The new method offers a way to distinguish conditions at different latitudes, as well as between the day and night sides of a planet. Eventually, this approach could help scientists investigate atmospheric structures on smaller scales, bringing them closer to mapping weather patterns on worlds far beyond our solar system. Dr. Wakeford said: "Having this very robust mathematical model that we can apply to this state-of-the-art data is incredibly exciting. The results are a really beautiful demonstration of the dynamics that are going on in these multidimensional and multifaceted worlds." top.title: NASA’s Curiosity rover reveals a spectacular new view of Mars with a mystery on the horizon
top.summary: NASA’s Curiosity rover has revealed a spectacular new view of mysterious, wind-carved cliffs on Mars that may hold evidence of ancient volcanic activity. With the rover approaching these unusual formations, scientists hope to uncover the secrets behind their strange appearance in 2027.
top.text: NASA's Curiosity rover has captured a spectacular new panorama of Mars, providing its clearest look yet at a series of mysterious cliffs shaped by wind. Scientists have been eager to examine these distant formations up close, and the latest images offer an exciting preview of what lies ahead. Taken at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time, the scene reveals striking blue tones across the foreground while morning sunlight illuminates rugged cliffs known as yardangs along the horizon. Curiosity recorded the panorama using its Mastcam on August 11, during the mission's 4,982nd Martian day, or sol. Six separate photographs were transmitted to Earth and combined to create the sweeping view. Unlike most Mastcam photographs, the images were processed without white balancing, allowing the scene to retain the distinctive colors and lighting of the Martian morning. The yardangs stretch approximately 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern portion of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been climbing since 2014. The rover recently achieved a major milestone, gaining 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) in elevation, a greater climb than any other rover has completed on Mars. As Curiosity continues toward these unusual formations, researchers anticipate increasingly detailed views of the cliffs. More importantly, they hope that examining the rocks firsthand will help explain how the remarkable landscape developed. Mount Sharp contains numerous layers of sedimentary rock, each preserving evidence from a different chapter of Martian history. Investigating these layers has helped scientists reconstruct a time billions of years ago when lakes and streams existed in this region of Mars. As the planet's environment changed, those bodies of water eventually disappeared, leaving deposits of salty minerals behind. Once additional material stopped accumulating on the mountain, powerful winds may have gradually eroded portions of the existing rock, carving out the distinctive yardangs visible today. Yet the unusual appearance of this particular layer has raised questions about its origins. Its color differs from the surrounding terrain, and its rock layers are tilted in an unexpected direction. Scientists suspect that processes beyond ordinary wind erosion may have contributed to its formation. "The yardang layer looks out of place. It's the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on," said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. "But that's what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions." Curiosity is now in the second year of its fifth extended mission, which began with an investigation of unusual spiderweb-like boxwork ridges. Over roughly the next year, the rover will continue traveling through rock layers containing abundant sulfates and carbonates, minerals that provide evidence of ancient drying conditions on Mars. Mission scientists aim to reach the bottom of the yardang formations sometime in 2027. Once there, Curiosity should be able to examine the mysterious cliffs using its robotic arm, gathering unique measurements that could help determine how they formed and reveal more about the environmental changes that shaped Mars billions of years ago. top.title: Music can enhance the flavor of your food
top.summary: The moment we take a sip of our morning coffee or our first bite of lunch, the brain begins interpreting what we taste. Is it sweet? Sour? Or something else entirely? But the brain does not create flavor based solely on signals from the tongue. That is the finding of a new study from the Department of Food Science, published in Scientific Reports.

top.title: This bird flies thousands of miles, but its wings have a catch
top.summary: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected trade-off in the wings of the European nightjar, a bird that migrates thousands of kilometers but sacrifices high-speed flight efficiency to hunt insects with remarkable agility. Even more surprisingly, it generates thrust on the upward wingbeat, a technique that could inspire new flying technologies.
top.text: A bird that migrates thousands of miles has revealed a surprising secret about how wings work. Scientists have discovered that European nightjars sacrifice flight efficiency for agility and use an unexpected wingbeat technique previously associated mainly with bats and insects. The European nightjar ( Caprimulgus europaeus ) is a nighttime hunter that makes an extraordinary annual migration between Europe and southern Africa. Yet the wings that carry it across vast distances must also perform a very different task: helping the bird catch insects while flying slowly and making sharp turns. Scientists at Lund University have discovered that these competing demands come with a surprising trade-off. Although the nightjar is built to handle long migrations, its wings are not perfectly optimized for efficient flight at higher speeds. To investigate how nightjars fly, researchers studied the birds in a wind tunnel, recording their movements at different speeds and measuring the patterns of airflow left behind their wings. The experiments revealed that the nightjar's broad wing tips, which likely help it maneuver during slow flight, become a disadvantage as the bird flies faster. At higher speeds, its wings generate lift less efficiently. Lift is the aerodynamic force that helps keep a bird airborne. The findings challenge the assumption that birds traveling enormous distances must have wings optimized primarily for efficient long-distance flight. "This runs counter to the intuitive image of a long-distance migrant as a perfectly optimized flying machine. Instead, the nightjar's wings appear to be a compromise between several different demands. The bird can fly slowly and maneuver while hunting, but the trade-off is reduced efficiency in lift generation at higher speeds," says Christoffer Johansson, associate professor at Lund University. The researchers also uncovered another surprising feature of the nightjar's flight. Even as the bird raises its wings during the upward portion of each wingbeat, it continues to generate thrust, the force that helps propel it forward. This is unusual because such an active upward wing movement, known as an upstroke, has previously been linked mainly to the flight mechanics of bats and insects rather than birds. The discovery suggests that animals with very different evolutionary histories may have developed similar aerodynamic solutions to the challenges of flying. "What's interesting is that the same type of aerodynamic solution seems to appear in quite different animals. This suggests that the upstroke does not have to be merely a passive or lift generating part of the wingbeat. It can be actively used to generate thrust when the wings cannot be folded very much," says Christoffer Johansson. The results offer a broader lesson about how evolution shapes animals that depend on the same body structures for different activities. Rather than producing wings perfectly suited to one purpose, evolution can favor designs that balance several competing needs. For the nightjar, that means combining the ability to migrate across continents with the agility required to hunt insects at low speeds. Understanding these compromises could also lead to improvements in aviation technology, particularly drones and other robotic aircraft that use flapping wings. Like birds, these machines may face mechanical restrictions on how much their wings can fold during each wingbeat. Learning how nightjars generate thrust during the upstroke could help engineers develop more effective ways to move through the air. Researchers now hope to determine whether this unusual flight mechanism is widespread among other birds and flying animals or whether it represents a more specialized adaptation. "We now want to investigate how common this way of generating force is among other birds and flying animals. It could help us understand which aerodynamic principles are specific to the nightjar and which are more general. This knowledge may also inspire the development of new types of flapping aircraft," Christoffer Johansson concludes. Materials provided by Lund University . top.title: A 24-year study uncovers a surprising climate benefit beneath forests
top.summary: Scientists have discovered that some forest soils are becoming surprisingly better at removing methane from the atmosphere as temperatures rise and rainfall declines. A study spanning up to 24 years found methane absorption increasing by an average of 3% annually, challenging previous predictions about climate change's effects on forests.
top.text: Forest soils are playing a surprisingly powerful role in removing methane from the atmosphere, and new findings suggest that certain effects of climate change could make them even better at it. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming, but microorganisms living in the soil can break it down before it builds up in the air. Scientists from the University of Göttingen and the Baden-Württemberg Forest Research Institute (FVA) analyzed the world's most comprehensive collection of long-term measurements of methane absorption by forest soils. Their findings revealed an unexpected trend: under certain climate conditions that could become more common in the future, forest soils can actually increase the amount of methane they remove from the atmosphere. The researchers examined measurements collected from 13 forest sites in southwestern Germany over periods of up to 24 years. On average, the amount of methane absorbed by the soils increased by approximately 3% annually. The researchers linked this rise to declining rainfall and warmer temperatures, which create conditions that make it easier for methane to enter the soil and be broken down by microorganisms. The findings, published in Agricultural and Forest Meteorology , challenge previous research suggesting that climate change is generally reducing the ability of forest soils to absorb methane. To understand how methane absorption changes over time, the researchers examined an extensive collection of soil gas measurements gathered through the FVA's long-running monitoring program. The measurements included soil gas profiles, which reveal the chemical composition of gases trapped in the soil at different depths. Every two weeks, researchers collected air samples through thin tubes installed beneath the ground and analyzed them in a laboratory. This repeated sampling allowed scientists to track changes in methane concentrations over many years. To confirm their findings, the team also used an independent measurement technique involving airtight chambers placed directly on the soil surface. By monitoring how gas concentrations changed inside these chambers, the researchers could determine whether the soil was absorbing methane and calculate how much was being removed. Combining these methods gave the scientists a detailed picture of methane uptake across the forest sites and how it responded to changing environmental conditions. Although methane absorption varied considerably between the 13 locations, a clear overall pattern emerged. Forest soils in southwestern Germany were particularly effective at removing methane from the atmosphere during periods of lower rainfall and higher temperatures. "Our long-term data shows that climate change does not necessarily have a negative impact on how much methane forest soils absorb. While the largest study to date from the US found a decline in methane uptake of up to 80 percent due to increasing rainfall, our significantly more comprehensive field study in south-western Germany found the opposite, " explains Professor Martin Maier at Göttingen University's Department of Crop Sciences, who led the study and was previously involved in the FVA's soil gas monitoring program. "We observed a significant long-term increase in methane uptake in the forest areas we studied." The explanation lies partly in how water moves through the ground. When soil becomes saturated with moisture, water fills many of the tiny spaces between soil particles, making it more difficult for gases to move through them. Drier soil contains more pores filled with air, allowing atmospheric methane to travel deeper into the ground. Once methane enters the soil, microorganisms use it as an energy source, breaking it down in the process. Rising temperatures can slightly accelerate this microbial activity, allowing the organisms to consume methane more quickly. Together, these two effects help explain why warmer temperatures and reduced rainfall were associated with greater methane absorption in the forests studied. The results offer a different perspective from several major international research reviews. These analyses, known as meta-analyses, combine findings from numerous individual studies to identify broader patterns. Many have concluded that methane absorption by forest soils is declining. However, the German study suggests that the relationship between climate change and methane uptake is more complicated than those overall trends indicate. While increasing rainfall can reduce methane absorption by limiting the movement of gas through soil, drier conditions can produce the opposite effect. The findings do not mean that climate change is beneficial for forests overall. Instead, they demonstrate that its effects on methane absorption can differ considerably depending on local temperatures, rainfall patterns, and soil conditions. The researchers emphasize that these regional differences make long-term monitoring especially important. Shorter studies or analyses that combine measurements from widely different environments may miss gradual changes that only become apparent after years of observation. "Our results make it clear that taking a series of measurements over many years and running monitoring programs are indispensable for assessing the real effects of climate change," says Maier. top.title: First drug-focused guideline outlines newer treatments for primary biliary cholangitis
top.summary: For the first time, a joint guideline from the American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) and American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) evaluates newer medications for primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), the most common cholestatic disease in adults. Published in Gastroenterology and HEPATOLOGY, the guideline provides evidence-based recommendations for diagnosis and treatment.

top.title: Potassium binder may ease the burden of dietary potassium restriction in people on dialysis
top.summary: Dietary potassium restriction is important for managing hyperkalemia, or high blood potassium levels, in individuals on maintenance hemodialysis, but it imposes a substantial day-to-day burden. Results from a recent clinical trial indicate that adding the potassium binder sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) may help. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

top.title: Fruits and vegetables outperform medication for treating metabolic acidosis in chronic kidney disease
top.summary: In people with chronic kidney disease (CKD), oral sodium bicarbonate is a standard treatment for metabolic acidosis (too much acid buildup in the body), but results from a recent clinical trial indicate that dietary acid reduction with base-producing fruits and vegetables may be a better option. The findings will be presented at ASN Kidney Week 2026, Oct. 22–25.

top.title: Liver tumors form without detectable driver mutations in mice, revealing epigenetic route
top.summary: Cancers can develop through epigenetic pathways even without driver gene mutations (DGMs), according to a study from Science Tokyo. Researchers uncovered the YAP1–TEAD–TET1 axis, which triggers DNA demethylation and activates multiple oncogenes in hepatocellular carcinoma. Suppressing TET1 reduced tumor formation in mice, while analysis of human liver disease data supported the relevance of these findings. This study reveals an alternative epigenetic route to cancer development and offers new insights into DGM-negative cancers.

top.title: How L-carnitine, found in red meat and exercise supplements, may amplify inflammation
top.summary: In a study published Oct. 19 in Cell, Yale researchers identified a previously unknown mechanism by which a nutrient abundant in red meat and commonly used in exercise supplements may amplify inflammation.

top.title: Children who eat more ultraprocessed foods show stronger brain responses to appetizing foods
top.summary: Children who eat more ultraprocessed foods (UPFs) show stronger responses in the brain's reward network when viewing images of appetizing foods—and these brain responses are linked to increases in body fat one year later.

top.title: Seabird family tree predicts which species accumulate plastic better than diet, global analysis finds
top.summary: What seabirds eat might seem like a good starting point for identifying species that tend to accumulate plastic in their digestive systems. Yet a recent global analysis suggests that mapping the evolutionary relatives of birds could offer better clues than their diets or feeding methods alone.

top.title: New long‑clawed British dinosaur is the first of its kind in Europe
top.summary: The fossilized skull of a new species of mysterious meat-eating dinosaur from the Isle of Wight has been rediscovered in the collections of the Natural History Museum after over 100 years in storage.

top.title: Stanford’s new microscope reveals living cells like never before
top.summary: Stanford scientists have developed a revolutionary microscope that reveals the hidden inner workings of living cells in real time, without the fluorescent labels that can interfere with observations. The breakthrough could provide new insights into cancer, infectious diseases, and how drugs interact with cells.
top.text: A new microscope developed at Stanford University allows scientists to watch the tiny structures inside living cells move and interact in real time, providing an exceptionally detailed view without the fluorescent labels typically used to make these structures visible. Researchers at Stanford have created a powerful new imaging system that reveals the inner workings of living cells with remarkable clarity. By combining two advanced microscopy techniques, the instrument achieves a resolution of approximately 120 nanometers, an unprecedented level of detail for an approach that does not require fluorescent labels. Known as Interferometric Image Scanning Microscopy (iISM), the technology makes it possible to observe multiple cellular structures simultaneously while they move, change, and respond to their surroundings. Scientists can also investigate what happens when cells encounter drugs or disease causing organisms, potentially uncovering biological processes that have been difficult to study. The breakthrough, described in the Nature portfolio journal Light: Science and Applications , could lead to advances in cancer research, drug development, infectious disease studies, and investigations of how plants interact with microorganisms. "This new microscope provides a fantastic new view into the cell, where you can see the tiny structures and machines in the cell moving, changing, and interacting without having to add fluorescence to observe them," said senior author W.E. Moerner, the Harry S. Mosher Professor of Chemistry in Stanford's School of Humanities and Sciences. "It's a wonderful look into these complex little cellular boxes that drive our life." One of the most important advantages of the new microscope is its ability to reveal cellular activity without relying on fluorescent markers. Many existing microscopy techniques use fluorescent substances to highlight specific structures inside cells. Although these methods have transformed biological research, they come with limitations. Researchers can generally label only a small number of structures at once, making it difficult to observe how different components interact across an entire cell. Fluorescent signals can also fade during observation through a process known as photobleaching. In addition, introducing the labels can be challenging, and some markers may alter the behavior of the very structures scientists want to study. The Stanford system avoids these problems by imaging cells without fluorescent labels. This allows researchers to follow numerous cellular components over extended periods while observing their activity in a more natural setting. Another advantage is that iISM requires substantially less illumination power than comparable label-free methods that produce high-contrast images. Lower light exposure reduces the possibility of photodamage, which occurs when the light used for imaging harms living cells or interferes with their normal functions. Although other specialized microscopes can achieve finer resolution, the combination of detailed imaging, gentle illumination, and extended observation makes iISM particularly valuable for studying living biological systems. The researchers emphasize that their technology is intended to complement fluorescence microscopy rather than replace it. First author Michelle Kueppers, a postdoctoral scholar in Moerner's laboratory, explained that combining the strengths of different imaging approaches could help scientists answer previously inaccessible questions. "Every method has its advantages and disadvantages, and we believe in a complementary implementation in the future," Kueppers said. "If we use the strengths of fluorescence for molecular specificity and the strength of iISM for label-free context and dynamics, we can really start tackling questions that have been difficult to address before." The breakthrough comes from bringing together two different microscopy technologies, each with its own advantages. Moerner received the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his pioneering contributions to super-resolution fluorescence microscopy. He specifically recruited Kueppers to Stanford because of her doctoral research involving a technique called "interferometric scattering microscopy." This method relies on a familiar property of light: scattering. Light changes direction when it encounters tiny particles. The same basic phenomenon explains why the sky appears blue. As sunlight passes through Earth's atmosphere, molecules, dust, and water droplets scatter its different wavelengths. Shorter blue wavelengths scatter more strongly than longer red wavelengths, producing the blue color we see overhead. Interferometric scattering microscopy takes advantage of this behavior on a much smaller scale. A laser illuminates a cell, causing tiny structures inside it to scatter some of the incoming light. Because the scattered signal is extremely weak, a second laser beam is used to amplify it through interference, allowing the microscope to detect structures that would otherwise be difficult to observe. The Stanford team improved this approach by combining it with technology adapted from advanced confocal microscopes. Traditional confocal microscopes use a small opening called a pinhole and a single detector to isolate light from a selected area. More advanced versions replace that arrangement with camera-based detector arrays capable of collecting multiple views of the same region. The researchers incorporated an array detector into their new microscope, allowing it to collect more light than a conventional system built around a pinhole and single detector. The advantage of collecting multiple perspectives is similar to the way human vision works. Our two eyes observe the world from slightly different positions, helping the brain distinguish nearby objects from those farther away. The Stanford microscope uses a related principle, but instead of relying on just two perspectives, its detector array gathers tens to hundreds of views. The researchers developed a computational method that combines these measurements to generate images with improved sharpness, contrast, depth information, and precision. By merging the strengths of interferometric scattering microscopy and advanced detector arrays, the team created an instrument capable of resolving structures as small as approximately 120 nanometers. For perspective, a nanometer is one billionth of a meter. At this scale, researchers can examine extremely small cellular structures and follow their movements and interactions. Crucially, the microscope achieves this resolution without sacrificing imaging speed or requiring intense laser illumination. Scientists can therefore observe living cells for longer periods while minimizing the risk of disturbing or damaging them. Moerner and Kueppers are continuing to refine the instrument, with the goal of eventually making it accessible to scientists across many areas of biology. One project uses the microscope to observe interactions among plant cells, fungi, and bacteria as they happen. By watching these organisms interact in real time, researchers hope to gain a clearer understanding of the complex relationships between plants and microbes. top.title: Legal encounters may offer overlooked opportunities for suicide prevention, analysis suggests
top.summary: Picture a forlorn man walking into a lawyer's office after his marriage has collapsed. The bank is threatening foreclosure, and his finances are in tatters. His problems may be legal on paper, but in person they can look far more complicated: panic, shame or the numb resignation of someone who can no longer imagine a way out. He did not come for counseling, and his lawyer is not a therapist. Still, the attorney may be sitting beside him at the worst moment of his life—with a chance to help before despair slides into tragedy.

top.title: Illegal fishing is thriving in African waters—a satellite system could help change that
top.summary: A patrol boat off the coast of Gabon intercepted three trawlers in July 2026, inside the Grand Sud Reserve. This is one of West and Central Africa's largest marine reserves, where industrial trawling is banned. None of the trawlers held a valid license. The patrol found them because analysts at the nonprofit Global Fishing Watch had studied satellite data and worked out where to look.

top.title: More young people are being recruited as 'money mules' by organized crime groups, new analysis reveals
top.summary: More than 8,900 people aged under 30 were arrested for money laundering offenses in England and Wales between 2020 and 2025. That's more than six in 10 of all money laundering arrests recorded during the period.

top.title: Hypnosis may help relieve stomach pain
top.summary: Stomach pain and other gastrointestinal complaints are common among children and adolescents. When symptoms recur over a long period, the cause may be a form of DGBI (disorders of gut-brain interaction), in which communication between the brain and the gut does not function as it should. This can affect both intestinal motility and the way pain is perceived.

top.title: Childhood adversity patterns reveal different links to hopelessness and drug or alcohol cravings
top.summary: Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are known to increase the risk of substance use problems later in life. New research from George Mason University's College of Public Health suggests that the specific types of adversity a young person faces may be associated with different vulnerabilities to those risks.

top.title: FDA patient, consumer reps often tied to pharma-funded groups
top.summary: Patient and consumer representatives advising U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) expert panels might actually be a Trojan horse for the pharmaceutical industry, a new study says.

top.title: Horror’s monsters find new meaning with queer and trans audiences – how ‘Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma’ dissects identity
top.summary: Horror as a genre has traditionally been rife with transphobia and homophobia. But LGBTQ+ fans love it anyway.
top.text: Queer horror is having a moment. The recent film “ Leviticus ” (2026), a harrowing allegory for conversion therapy , was a critical hit. Meanwhile, Ryan Murphy’s undeniably gay “ American Horror Story ” returned to TV this fall, offering a campier approach to the genre. But queer people’s fascination with horror is by no means new. For trans and queer viewers, horror has long acted as a mirror to reflect on complex personal questions of identity and embodiment. Another new film, Jane Schoenbrun’s “ Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma ” (2026), explores queer people’s relationship with horror. Schoenbrun’s film isn’t really a horror movie; it’s a movie about horror movies . The protagonist, a young auteur named Kris, is rebooting an old slasher franchise, “Camp Miasma.” The franchise has aged poorly, and she wants to update the film for a contemporary audience. “This part’s transphobic!” Kris mutters while watching the original film. But Kris is also helplessly obsessed with “Camp Miasma,” and Schoenbrun’s film suggests that it’s precisely the slasher’s troubling, problematic elements that have enthralled her. As both a trans studies scholar and a longtime horror fan, I know how she feels. In fact, Kris’ complicated relationship with “Camp Miasma” may feel deeply familiar for many queer and trans viewers. Horror has produced some of the most objectionable queer- and trans-coded characters in cinema history. These portrayals of LGBTQ+ people as monstrous and pathological can be found in films ranging from the low-budget slashers that inspired Schoenbrun – most notably “ Sleepaway Camp ” (1983) – to Oscar winners such as “ The Silence of the Lambs ” (1991). Yet queer and trans audiences have often found themselves strangely drawn to these films and to the horror genre overall . Why does a genre that has treated LGBTQ+ people so poorly keep them coming back? No one’s 20s and 30s look the same. You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our Quarter Life series has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone. ‘Heartstopper’ is helping LGBTQ+ fans find hope and community across time and space Childhood experiences of LGBTQ+ stigma can harm romantic relationships decades later – psychologists explain how to reconnect with yourself and your partner Heated Rivalry shows how queer joy can disrupt hockey’s culture of masculinity Queerness is baked into the very structure of the horror genre. Film scholar Robin Wood summarized the horror formula as “Normality is threatened by the Monster.” As Wood points out, the social order that represents “normality” is often tied to heteronormative structures like the nuclear family and the heterosexual couple. Horror stages gleeful attacks on this order: Think of the family under siege by malevolent spirits, or the straight camp counselors hacked to bits after having sex. Such themes may resonate strongly for queers who find their goals and desires in tension with a society primarily built around cisgender, heterosexual life paths. Beyond its social elements, horror also offers queer and trans people a personal encounter with an aspect of themselves that they may find confusing or even upsetting: their bodies. Feminist scholar Carol Clover argued that horror is a “ body genre ,” meaning it is intended to activate a bodily response in the viewer. Often, one of the ways horror elicits this physical response is through the visceral, violent onscreen deformation of bodies. In body horror , the human body is depicted as an unruly, often disgusting and always vulnerable accumulation of flesh , blood and guts. Such images can mirror and affirm the difficult feelings that many queer and trans folks have experienced with regard to embodiment, their distress surrounding the forms their bodies take or the desires they feel. Horror’s depiction of monsters and monstrous bodies have allowed many queer and trans people to take ownership over their experiences of personal pain and social stigma. As trans theorist Susan Stryker put it, “I want to lay claim to the dark power of my monstrous identity without using it as a weapon against others or being wounded by it myself.” Other queer and trans writers, however, have asked about the limits of identifying with monstrosity. “How does building an identity on reclaiming the boogeyman affect the psyche ?” wonders critic Grace Byron. Horror, after all, centers on violence, brutality, fear and even death. Identifying with these forces might feel powerful in the moment, but it doesn’t necessarily help reckon with the real violence that led LGBTQ+ people to identify with them in the first place. When I teach horror , my students and I talk about how we might approach some of the most transphobic figures in the horror canon. Instead of identifying with these “monsters,” we try to think critically about the conditions that created them. Take the trans-coded serial killer Buffalo Bill, from “The Silence of the Lambs.” Scholar Cael Keegan argues that “The Silence of the Lambs” raises issues of state violence against transgender people. Similarly, scholar Grace Lavery reads Buffalo Bill as a victim of medical gatekeeping , which bars lifesaving gender-related care from those who need it. Rather than either rejecting characters like Buffalo Bill or embracing their monstrosity, queer viewers and their allies could instead ask what these characters show about the structural conditions that keep queer and trans people at the margins of society. When my students approach horror, I encourage them to consider the strategy that queer theorist José Esteban Muñoz offers for minority groups engaging with harmful representations in dominant culture: disidentification . For Muñoz, to “disidentify” means refusing to see yourself in images that degrade you, yet still finding ways of making those violent representations generative for your own thinking, dreaming and living. “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” is about disidentifying with horror. It acknowledges the harmful, long-standing transphobia of the genre. And it is also frank about the disturbing prevalence of sexual violence in horror, both onscreen and behind the scenes . But the queer characters in “Camp Miasma” – both in Schoenbrun’s film and in its fictional counterpart – still manage to connect with themselves and their bodies. And I think they do this not just by watching horror, but by watching themselves watch horror. So perhaps the draw of horror for queer and trans people isn’t just that it lets them identify with onscreen monsters or victims of violence. It’s that it gives them the opportunity to reflect on these identifications – and to reject them or transform them. In the process of finding meaning in horror’s monstrous worlds, queer and trans people tap into their own power to respond to the monstrous world around them.

top.title: Intermittent fasting plus exercise boosts fat loss and fitness in 12-week obesity trial
top.summary: A research team led by the Joint University Institute for Sport and Health (iMUDS) at the University of Granada, in collaboration with the Granada Institute for Biomedical Research and the Biomedical Research Network Center, has studied the effects of combining intermittent fasting and supervised exercise in people with obesity as part of the TEMPUS project.

top.title: International study helps support FDA approval of HIV drug for newborns
top.summary: An international study conducted through the International Maternal Pediatric Adolescent AIDS Clinical Trials (IMPAACT) Network, including researchers at the University of California San Diego, helped inform the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) recent approval of dolutegravir, a second-generation integrase inhibitor, for the treatment of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) in newborns from birth. The study, published in The Lancet HIV, identified a dosing regimen that achieves appropriate drug levels in full-term newborns, supporting the use of dolutegravir to treat HIV from the first days of life.

top.title: East Asia's summer rain belt has shifted north over decades, reshaping rain and heat risks
top.summary: A joint research team from KAIST and the APEC Climate Center has found that the East Asian summer front has migrated north over the past half century, with the shift exceeding 200 km (124 miles) in late summer. This raises the risk that the Korean Peninsula will experience heavy rain and heat stress at the same time. The findings suggest that summer disaster planning should address flood prevention and heat-illness management together, through late September.

top.title: Study finds lower rates of overweight among vegan-fed cats
top.summary: A large-scale survey has found cats fed vegan diets had lower rates of obesity and related health problems than those fed conventional meat-based diets.
